# Gradients of Vector Fields
A **vector field** is an assignment of a vector to each point in a space. On a
Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ we can visualize the field as a collection of
arrows with given magnitudes and directions, each attached to a point on the
plane.

<!-- TODO: image "Pasted image 20250715150758.png" not found in vault -->
*Figure: Vector field visualization.*

The **gradient** of a scalar-valued function $f$ of several variables which is
differentiable at a point $p$ is the vector $\nabla f(p)$ giving the direction
and the rate of fastest increase of $f$ at $p$. Letting $p$ vary, $\nabla f$ is
a vector field.

# Cartesian Gradient

:::{.definition data-title="Euclidean Gradient"}

In $n$-dimensional Cartesian coordinates with Euclidean metric the gradient, at
any point where $f$ is differentiable, is given by
$$
\nabla f:=\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{{\partial f}}{\partial x_{i}}\boldsymbol{i}_{i},
$$
where $\boldsymbol{i}_{j}$ is the standard unit vector in the direction of the
$x_{j}$ coordinate.

:::

This result is written in standard basis notation but alternatively could be
written in column vector notation as
$$
\nabla f:=\begin{bmatrix}
\frac{{\partial f}}{\partial x_{1}} \\
\vdots  \\
\frac{{\partial f}}{\partial x_{n}}
\end{bmatrix}=\left[ \frac{{\partial f}}{\partial x_{i}} \right]_{i=1,..,n}.
$$

:::{.example}

**Cartesian Gradient.** Consider the function $f(x,y,z)=2x+3xy^2-\sin (z)$. The
gradient is
$$
\nabla f=\begin{bmatrix}
2+3y^2 \\
6xy \\
-\cos(z)
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

:::

# General Coordinate Gradient
Consider general coordinates in an $n$-dimensional space
$x=(x^i)_{i=1,\dots,n}$ and let $f$ be a scalar-valued function
$f(x):=f(x^1, \dots, x^n)$ differentiable at the point of interest. The
gradient of $f$ is given by
$$
\nabla f= \frac{{\partial f}}{\partial x^i}g^{ij}\boldsymbol{e}_{j},
$$
where $\boldsymbol{e}_{i}=\frac{{\partial \boldsymbol{x}}}{\partial x^i}$ is
the (unnormalized) local *tangent basis* and $\boldsymbol{e}^i=dx^i$ is the
dual *cobasis* of differentials, $g^{ij}$ is the *inverse metric tensor*, and
the Einstein summation convention implies summation over $i$ and $j$.

:::{.example}

**Polar Coordinates.** Take $(x^1,x^2)=(r,\theta)$ with
$\boldsymbol{x}=(r\cos\theta,\, r\sin\theta)$. The tangent basis is
$\boldsymbol{e}_r=\hat{\boldsymbol{r}}$ and
$\boldsymbol{e}_\theta=r\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$, and the metric is
$g=\mathrm{diag}(1,r^2)$ so $g^{-1}=\mathrm{diag}(1,r^{-2})$. Hence
$$
\nabla f = \frac{\partial f}{\partial r}\hat{\boldsymbol{r}}
+\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta}\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}.
$$

:::

The same computation gives the other standard cases.

| Coordinates | $\nabla f$ |
|---|---|
| Cylindrical $(\rho,\varphi,z)$ | $f_\rho\,\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}+\frac{1}{\rho}f_\varphi\,\hat{\boldsymbol{\varphi}}+f_z\,\hat{\boldsymbol{z}}$ |
| Spherical $(r,\theta,\varphi)$, $\theta$ the polar angle | $f_r\,\hat{\boldsymbol{r}}+\frac{1}{r}f_\theta\,\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}+\frac{1}{r\sin\theta}f_\varphi\,\hat{\boldsymbol{\varphi}}$ |

# Gradient Results

## Relationship to Total Derivative
The gradient is closely related to the **total derivative** $df$. For a
differentiable $f$, $df_p$ is the linear map with
$$
df_p(\boldsymbol{v})=\nabla f(p)\cdot\boldsymbol{v}\quad\text{for all }\boldsymbol{v},
$$
so $\nabla f(p)$ is the vector representing the linear functional $df_p$ via
the metric. In index notation $\nabla f=g^{-1}df$, which in an orthonormal basis
(e.g. Cartesian coordinates) reduces to the transpose
$$
\nabla f=df^T.
$$

## Directional Derivative

:::{.definition data-title="Directional Derivative"}

The derivative of $f$ at $p$ in the direction of a unit vector
$\boldsymbol{v}$ is
$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial \boldsymbol{v}}(p)
:=\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(p+h\boldsymbol{v})-f(p)}{h}
=\nabla f(p)\cdot\boldsymbol{v},
$$
the second equality holding when $f$ is differentiable at $p$.

:::

## Geometric Properties

:::{.theorem data-title="Geometry of the Gradient"}

Let $f$ be differentiable at $p$ with $\nabla f(p)\neq 0$. Then:

- $\nabla f(p)$ points in the direction of steepest ascent of $f$, and
  $|\nabla f(p)|$ is the maximal rate of increase.
- $\nabla f(p)$ is orthogonal to the level set $\{f=f(p)\}$ through $p$.

If $p$ is an interior local extremum of $f$, then $\nabla f(p)=0$.

:::

:::{.proof}

For a unit vector $\boldsymbol{v}$ the
[[cauchy-schwartz-inequality|Cauchy-Schwarz inequality]] gives
$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial \boldsymbol{v}}=\nabla f\cdot\boldsymbol{v}
\le |\nabla f|,
$$
with equality iff $\boldsymbol{v}=\nabla f/|\nabla f|$. If $\gamma(t)$ is a
curve in the level set with $\gamma(0)=p$ then $f(\gamma(t))$ is constant, so
by the [[chain-rule|chain rule]] $\nabla f(p)\cdot\gamma'(0)=0$. Finally, at an
interior local maximum (or minimum) every directional derivative vanishes, as
$t\mapsto f(p+t\boldsymbol{v})$ has a local extremum at $t=0$. Thus
$\nabla f(p)\cdot\boldsymbol{v}=0$ for all $\boldsymbol{v}$, i.e.
$\nabla f(p)=0$.

:::

## Calculation Rules
For differentiable $f,g$, a constant $c$ and a differentiable $h:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$:

- $\nabla(f+g)=\nabla f+\nabla g$ and $\nabla(cf)=c\nabla f$,
- $\nabla(fg)=f\nabla g+g\nabla f$,
- $\nabla(h\circ f)=h'(f)\nabla f$.

# Related Notions
Applying other differential operators to $\nabla f$ gives the
[[divergence|divergence]] of the gradient, which is the
[[laplace-operator|Laplacian]] $\Delta f=\nabla\cdot\nabla f$. The matrix of
second derivatives of $f$ is the Hessian, see
[[jacobian-and-hessian|Jacobian and Hessian]]. Further identities are collected
in [[vector-calculus-identities|vector calculus identities]].

Vector fields of the form $\boldsymbol{F}=\nabla f$ are called *conservative*,
with potential $f$. Gradients also appear in physical laws such as Fourier's law
of diffusion, where the flux is $-\nabla u$, and in optimisation, where gradient
descent follows $-\nabla f$.
